children.text: Completed around

, the Church of San Agustin is a masterpiece of Philippine Earthquake Baroque architecture, its 24 massive buttresses having withstood earthquakes for centuries. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in
, it sits just
30 minutes
from Laoag, making it a must-see stop on any Ilocos trip.
Paoay Church's official name is the Church of San Agustin. Augustinian friars began construction around
and completed it around
. In

it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List together with the San Agustin Church in Intramuros, Manila, Miagao Church in Iloilo, and Santa Maria Church in Ilocos Sur, under the collective title "Baroque Churches of the Philippines." The Philippine government had already designated it a National Cultural Treasure earlier, in
What makes this church special is the massive buttresses on both sides, which you can see at a glance. Twenty-four buttresses about

thick lean against the walls on both sides and at the back of the church. It is regarded as the most dramatic example of the so-called "Earthquake Baroque" style, devised to keep buildings from collapsing in the earthquake-prone Philippines. It is said to have been built of coral stone and brick joined with a mortar of lime mixed with sugarcane juice and other ingredients, and the stepped gable at the top of the facade recalls the towers of Asian temples, giving the church a unique look that blends Gothic, Baroque, and Asian styles.
The detached three-story bell tower beside the church had its cornerstone laid in
. It is said that Katipunan revolutionaries used it as a lookout during the Philippine Revolution of
, and guerrillas did the same in World War II. The church is especially beautiful when the west-facing facade glows golden at sunset, and at night during the Christmas season when the lights are on.
It suits travelers who enjoy historic architecture and photography, as well as families touring Ilocos Norte from a base in Laoag. The church itself takes just
1–2 hours
to see, but Paoay Lake, Malacañang of the North, the Marcos Museum in Batac, and the Suba sand dunes are all nearby, making it easy to combine into a full-day itinerary.
Parts of the church were damaged and repaired in the
and
earthquakes, and the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) restored the exterior walls and buttresses again from
to
June 2020
. The crew cleared the grass and trees covering the walls so the stone would not wear away, repaired the bell tower stairs and the entire roof, and returned the church to the Diocese of Laoag in
November 2020

, so the church looks quite different from photos taken in the 2010s, when the facade was covered with green plants. Right next to the church on its north side, the brick arches of the old convent (convento), whose roof is long gone, remain as ruins.

Don't just view the facade and leave — walk slowly around the sides and back of the church. The row of buttresses with their scroll-shaped ornaments is the church's true face, and looking up from the shade between them gives you a real sense of scale.
Shooting wide-angle from the far end of the front lawn lets you fit the whole church and the bell tower into one frame. Mornings are backlit, so photos come out best after

The interior is more modest than the exterior, but the cool air created by the thick walls and the simple altar leave an impression. During Mass, watch quietly from the back, and on weekends, when weddings are frequent, it's polite to check the schedule before entering.

blocks.title: Examine the coral-stone walls by the bell tower

children.text: Get close and you can see the coral stone embedded between the bricks, the moss, and the weathering left by 300 years. Scratching the walls or climbing on them damages the heritage site and should be avoided.

Around the plaza are stalls selling Inabel, the traditional Ilocano woven fabric, along with local specialties like garlic, bagoong (fermented fish sauce), and chicharon. Inabel table runners or handkerchiefs make easy, affordable gifts.

blocks.title: Pinakbet pizza at the cafe across from the church

children.text: Herencia Café, across from the church, has long been known for its "pinakbet pizza," topped with the Ilocano vegetable dish pinakbet. It's a great spot for a late lunch with a view of the church.

for adults (

The church's exterior walls are often lit up at night, and in
December
the plaza is crowded with Christmas decorations. In recent years, a light show (Northern Symphony of Lights) was held on evenings from
December–early January

, casting colored lights on the facade and bell tower while Christmas songs played, so check that year's schedule. It's also nice to stop by once more around dusk before heading back to your accommodation in Laoag.

Take a jeepney to Laoag (about
40 minutes
), check in to your accommodation, then explore the city
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly from Manila to Laoag International Airport (LAO), a flight of about
1 hour 10 minutes
. One-way fares run about
depending on the season. The airport is about
7 km
southwest of Laoag city center, reachable by tricycle or taxi in
15–20 minutes
; going straight from the airport to Paoay takes about
30 minutes
by car.

Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific together operate about 3 flights a day: Cebu Pacific has an early-morning flight, and Philippine Airlines has daytime and evening flights (schedules may change). There are no regular direct flights to Laoag from other cities such as Cebu or Davao, so you must connect through Manila.
Buses to Laoag run by Partas, Fariñas Transit, GV Florida, Maria de Leon, and others leave several times a day from Manila's Cubao, Sampaloc, Pasay, and other areas. The trip takes about
9–11 hours
, and fares run about

depending on the class (regular, deluxe, first class, super deluxe); sleeper buses with beds cost more. Overnight buses that leave at night and arrive in the morning are convenient. Instead of riding all the way to the Laoag terminal, you can get off at Batac and transfer to a jeepney or tricycle, which gets you to Paoay in about
10–15 minutes
Jeepneys (including air-conditioned modern jeepneys) run from Laoag city to Paoay via San Nicolas and Batac about every
30 minutes
. The ride takes about
40 minutes
and costs about
. Return jeepneys become scarce in the evening, so if you plan to stay late, ask about the last departure in advance. To cover several sites, chartering a tricycle for half a day (about
) or hiring a van with a driver is more efficient. A southern tour of Laoag, Paoay, and Batac by van starts from about
, and a full-day charter runs about
according to the provincial tourism guide.
From Vigan, take a Laoag-bound bus, get off at Batac, and transfer to a tricycle or jeepney; it takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
to reach Batac. From Baguio, Fariñas and Partas run Laoag-bound buses that take about
6–9 hours
, with first-class fares around
. If you're coming down from Pagudpud or Bangui in the north, go through Laoag and take the same jeepney.
From Manila, the route of about
460 km
takes the NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX expressways, then goes up MacArthur Highway from Rosario in La Union and passes through Vigan and Batac. Even without stops it takes about
7–9 hours
, so staying a night in Vigan and continuing the next day is a reasonable plan. From central Batac, about
10 minutes
more by car to the west brings you to the plaza in front of the church.
The Ilocos region has distinct dry and rainy seasons, even by Philippine standards.
November
through
April
is the dry season, with almost no rain and clear skies that make for great photos of the church. From
December–February
mornings and evenings are a pleasantly cool 20°C or so, which is good for walking, while in
March–May
midday temperatures climb to nearly 35°C, so the shadeless plaza gets quite hot.
From
June
through
October
, the southwest monsoon (habagat) brings frequent rain, and from
July–September
typhoons often pass through northern Luzon. Flights and buses to Laoag can be suspended when a typhoon hits, so it's wise to build extra time into your schedule during this period.
As for events, the feast of the church's patron saint, St. Augustine (around
August 28
), brings Mass and processions, and in
February
Laoag City holds the "Pamulinawen Festival" to mark its own patron saint's feast, packed with street parades and food stalls. Holy Week (the week before Easter) and
December
see a big rise in pilgrims and domestic travelers.
According to the Laoag station's climate normals (PAGASA, 1991–2020),
January
averages a high of
and a low of
, and the hottest month,
May
, has a high of
. Rainy days number only 1–2 a month in
January–April
, but rise to 17 in
August
, when monthly rainfall reaches about 594 mm.
Paoay town also has events you won't see elsewhere. On the day before Ash Wednesday (
February–early March

), the Guling-Guling Festival takes place: residents marked with a cross of white rice-flour paste on the forehead and dressed in traditional Inabel costumes dance and march to the plaza in front of the church. On
November 1
, the Tumba custom continues, in which food and photos of the deceased are laid out in a temporary hut (tumba) built of bamboo and palm leaves, and people pray until late at night.

Paoay town has a few small guesthouses and resorts, but for more choice and easier transport, staying in Laoag city, about
30 minutes
away by car, is most convenient. Laoag has many clean, mid-range hotels priced around
per night, and the large Fort Ilocandia resort beside the sand dunes south of the city is popular with families. A few quiet resort-style lodgings can also be found on the shore of Paoay Lake.

Ilocano food is known for being salty and strongly garlicky. The must-tries are Batac empanada (an orange-hued fried pastry of rice-flour dough filled with shredded green papaya, egg, and longganisa), bagnet (crispy fried pork), pinakbet (a vegetable stir-fry made with bagnet), dinengdeng (vegetables simmered in a broth of fermented fish paste, or bagoong), and longganisa (Ilocano-style sausage). The pinakbet pizza and bagnet pizza at Herencia Café in front of Paoay Church have long been famous among travelers, and the empanada stall street in downtown Batac (Riverside Empanadaan) is a favorite of locals, too.

Paoay is known for weaving inabel, the traditional Ilocano hand-loomed fabric, and for garlic farming, so many visitors buy Inabel blankets and table runners and Ilocos garlic as souvenirs at the stalls around the church. Most of the town's restaurants and shops are clustered around the church, so you can explore them on foot.
Admission to the church is free, but interior viewing is limited during Mass and weddings. Weddings are common on weekend mornings and late afternoons, so weekday afternoons are quieter.
As it is a place of worship, avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts. Bring a light shirt or scarf to cover up if needed.
The best time for photos is
3–5 PM
. The facade faces west, so afternoon sunlight lights it evenly. In the morning, start with the buttressed sides and the back.
Paoay town has few ATMs, so withdraw enough cash in Laoag beforehand. Stalls and tricycles accept cash only.
When chartering a tricycle or van, agree on the list of stops, the total fare, and the waiting time before you set off, to avoid disputes later.
The plaza has almost no shade at midday. Bring a hat, sunscreen, and about a liter of water.
If combining this with a 4x4 tour of the Suba sand dunes, visit the church first and head to the dunes late in the afternoon to avoid the hottest sand.
If you're also visiting Vigan, Paoay lies right along the Vigan–Laoag route, so it's efficient to stop by on the way.
Festival schedules and notices about tourist sites can be found on the
official Ilocos Norte website
Rates and operating hours for nearby attractions such as Malacañang of the North and the sand dunes are listed on the Ilocos Norte tourism office's
attraction rates guide
page.
The church is a cultural treasure over 300 years old. Climbing the buttresses, prying off bricks, or flying a drone without permission is prohibited and may be penalized.
During restoration or repair work, some areas may be covered with scaffolding or closed off. Check announcements from Paoay Church or the Ilocos Norte tourism office before visiting.
The ruins of the old convent next to the church were rated "unsafe" in a provincial government inspection after the
July 2022
Abra earthquake, and they were damaged again in the
October
earthquake. Bricks can fall, so don't lean on or climb the walls, and don't enter areas blocked off with ropes or signs.
There is a risk of heatstroke at midday in
March–May
. Drink water often, especially if combining this with a visit to the sand dunes.
During typhoon season from
July–September
, flights and buses are often canceled and coastal roads can flood. Check PAGASA forecasts and build a spare day into your schedule.
If someone around the plaza offers to "guide" you, confirm the fee up front, and feel free to politely decline if you don't want the service.
The church is a living place of worship where Mass is still held today. Please remember it is a place of prayer first, and a tourist attraction second.
About
15 minutes
from Laoag city, this is Ilocos's signature activity — racing across a desert-like dune field in a 4x4 jeep.
